clusters.text: While crashing protons together at nearly the speed of light, scientists at CERN found evidence of one of the most improbable decays of matter—so unlikely that it’s a phenomenon physicists have been hoping to observe for more than four decades. The collision produced numerous particles, including some known as neutral B mesons, and scientists found signals indicating that one of these had decayed into a muon and an antimuon. Mesons decay all the time. These tiny particles, smaller than atoms, arise from collisions between other particles and exist only briefly before transforming into other particles. Muons, on the other hand, are similar to the electrons found in atoms, but about 200 times heavier. Scientists study these particles and their decays to test the predictions of current physics and search for clues to unknown particles. The standard model—the sort of bible of particle physics—predicts that for every 10 billion decays of neutral B mesons, this transformation will occur once. In other words, even if scientists were to observe 10 billion of these particles decaying, they would expect to find, on average, only a single muon and antimuon. This discovery is the first time an experiment has obtained evidence of this phenomenon, the details of which the researchers have made available in a preprint on arXiv. “Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than 40 years,” Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team, said in a press release from CERN. “Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.” The extraordinary rarity of this process explains why it’s taken decades of research to arrive at this discovery. But upgrades to the Large Hadron Collider in 2024 also made observing this phenomenon possible. The revamp enabled faster data collection, and new machine-learning techniques allowed researchers “to suppress the vast background of processes that would have otherwise swamped the signals from these rare beauty-particle decays,” as CERN described it in its statement. This decay opens a new avenue for investigating the limits of what scientists have been able to observe. clusters.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in January California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison. "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter. The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president. Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday. clusters.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
clusters.snippet: The Delhi government has announced a four-month winter action plan, but experts say that won't be enough.
clusters.text: People exercise in a park in Delhi on Thursday, breathing in hazy, polluted air There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers. "The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher. She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air. Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable. Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality. The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it? This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes. Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures. Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern . This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere. For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution. Anti-smog guns sprinkle water to settle atmospheric dust in Delhi Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year.

The court observed that merely questioning the rights of minorities cannot constitute an offence and that the speech in question was protected under the right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 19 of the Constitution.The court further noted that while an elected representative raising concerns on foreign soil may, for some, raise questions of propriety or appear to depart from long-standing traditions of parliamentary democracy, that alone does not make such speech a criminal offence.It also observed that even if statements made by an elected representative were found to be inaccurate or unsubstantiated, the appropriate remedy lies in parliamentary debate and public discourse, where the truth can emerge through the free exchange of ideas. Reiterating its position, the court held that the speech attributed to Gandhi was protected under Article 19.The petition was filed under Section 528 (inherent powers of the High Court) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).The matter arose from an application filed before the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, MP/MLA Court, Varanasi, under Section 173(4) of the BNSS seeking registration of an FIR against Gandhi for his alleged “provocative” remarks on the Sikh community. clusters.snippet: Air India's Maharaja Club has launched its e commerce shop, where you can earn points for purchases via their Maharaja Shop. The post Air India launches The Maharaja Shop, a new way to earn Maharaja Points appeared first on Live From A Lounge .
also: Air India Turns Shopping Into Free Flight Rewards, Launches ‘The Maharaja Shop’ To Earn Points On Everyday
clusters.text: Air India has announced it is launching The Maharaja Shop, an online marketplace where Maharaja Club members can earn points on eligible purchases. The store covers everything from electronics and luggage to fragrances, home essentials, wellness products, watches and jewellery. Members can earn Maharaja Points on purchases and use them for Award Flights and Cabin Upgrades on Air India. It gives members another way to build a points balance without flying or using one of the programme’s existing partners. Air India’s new shop brings together a curated selection of Indian and international brands across multiple lifestyle categories. The website is themaharajashop.com and is being managed by Vernost, the travel and loyalty solutions company that also runs Axis Bank’s TravelEDGE programme, among others. Some of the product categories being sold to start off include Air India Merchandise, Mobile Phones, Laptop Accessories, Audio accessories and Travel products. Of course, more products will be added soon. The earning rate varies by product, with Maharaja Club points offered at INR 30 to INR 134 per 1 MC point. The most distinctive part of the launch is a collection of Air India merchandise available only through The Maharaja Shop. It includes Maharaja magnets and collectables, aircraft-inspired keychains, lapel pins, postcards, coasters and travel accessories. Surprisingly, the list is missing model aircraft. For frequent flyers and collectors, this is a way to buy Air India-branded items that may not be available elsewhere, while earning Maharaja Points on eligible purchases. The shop is open only to Maharaja Club members, though non-members can join the programme to shop. The shop joins a growing list of ways to earn Maharaja Points outside Air India flights. The programme now has more than 100 partners across airlines, hospitality, retail, lifestyle and financial services. Members can redeem points on Air India, Air India Express and 25 Star Alliance partner airlines. Air India also says eligible members have access to more than 1,100 lounges worldwide through their tier privileges. A dedicated shopping portal is a familiar feature of many loyalty programmes. clusters.text: Prayagraj: In a move expected to strengthen the city’s digital infrastructure and attract technology-driven investments, the Uttar Pradesh State Industrial Development Authority (UPSIDA) has issued a Letter of Intent (LoI) to Airtel Nxtra Private Limited for the allotment of 4.43 acres at Saraswati Hi-Tech City in Prayagraj to set up a 10 MW data centre.The LoI, issued on Nov 5, covers Plots 5 and 7 and involves a proposed investment of around Rs 220 crore. clusters.text: Ranchi: Dhanteras shopping in Ranchi is extending beyond traditional gold and silver purchases, with automobiles, electronics and property emerging as major choices for festive buyers. From SUVs and household appliances to residential flats, consumers are making high-value purchases, prompting businesses across sectors to anticipate a strong festive season.Rajkumar, head of sales at an automobile outlet, said, “Cars, priced between Rs 11 lakh and Rs 17 lakh, is among the most sought-after models this season, with around three-month waiting period.““In the past month, we have retailed around 1,100 vehicles and received bookings for another 1,500 ahead of Dhanteras. Customer enquiries continue until midnight, keeping our entire sales team occupied. Vehicles offering multiple fuel options, including petrol, CNG, hybrid and electric, are seeing particularly good demand. CNG models are frequently out of stock,” he said.Sri Krishna Agarwal, head of the electronics sub-committee of the Federation of Jharkhand Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FJCCI), expects the sector to generate around Rs 200 crore in turnover across Jharkhand. “Though e-commerce platforms attract price-sensitive customers throughout the year, Dhanteras brings many buyers back to physical stores. Mobile phones, televisions, refrigerators, washing machines, air fryers and induction cooktops are among the preferred purchases. Consumer offers and bonus schemes are also encouraging buyers,” he said.The real estate market is witnessing a preference for flats over independent houses. Alok Sarawagi, head of the FJCCI’s real estate sub-committee, said, “Buyers increasingly prioritise security, organised neighbourhoods and maintenance facilities.”For many households, Dhanteras is also an opportunity to make planned purchases. “Dhanteras is a good occasion for big purchases because festive offers make them more affordable.
